Epidemiology , Study design.question: 1) Epidemiology is the study of distribution and determinants of health-related events in:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Epidemiology studies health-related events in specified populations. It includes distribution, determinants and application to control health problems. It is a population-based science.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 2) The three basic components of epidemiology include disease frequency, distribution and:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Basic components are disease frequency, distribution and determinants. Disease frequency measures occurrence. Determinants explain why and how disease occurs.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 3) Disease frequency in epidemiology mainly answers:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Disease frequency measures amount of disease. It includes incidence, prevalence and mortality measures. It helps compare disease burden between populations.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 4) Distribution of disease mainly describes disease according to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Distribution describes who gets disease, where it occurs and when it occurs. These three axes are person, place and time. They are central to descriptive epidemiology.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 5) Determinants of disease mainly refer to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Determinants explain factors responsible for disease occurrence. They include biological, behavioural, environmental and social factors. Identifying determinants helps prevention.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 6) Which is a tool of measurement in epidemiology?
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Rate is one of the epidemiological tools of measurement. Ratio and proportion are also used. These tools quantify health events.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 7) A ratio compares:
Epidemiology , Study design.option2: Only old cases with new cases
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Ratio compares two quantities. The numerator may or may not be included in the denominator. Sex ratio is a common demographic example.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 8) A proportion means:
Epidemiology , Study design.option4: Numerator is completely unrelated to denominator
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: In a proportion, numerator is included in denominator. It expresses a part of the whole. Percentage is a common form of proportion.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 9) A rate usually includes:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Rate measures occurrence of an event in a population over time. The time factor makes it different from simple ratio or proportion. Incidence rate is a classical example.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 10) Incidence measures:
Epidemiology , Study design.option1: Old and new cases at one point
Epidemiology , Study design.option2: New cases during a specified period
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Incidence means new cases occurring in a defined population during a specified period. It measures risk of developing disease. It is useful for acute diseases and etiological study.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 11) Prevalence measures:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Prevalence includes all existing cases, old and new. It may be measured at a point or over a period. It reflects disease burden in a population.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 12) The relationship between prevalence, incidence and duration is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: The relationship is P = I × D. Prevalence rises when incidence is high or disease duration is long. It is especially useful in chronic diseases.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 13) In chronic disease, prevalence is usually:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Chronic diseases last for long duration. Therefore, old cases accumulate in the population. This makes prevalence much greater than incidence.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 14) In acute diseases, incidence and prevalence are usually:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Acute diseases have short duration. Cases do not remain for long in the population. Therefore, prevalence and incidence may be close.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 15) A sudden rise in new dengue cases is best measured by:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Incidence measures new cases over time. A sudden increase in dengue cases is captured by incidence. It is useful for outbreak monitoring.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 16) Total existing cases of hypertension in a city are best measured by:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Prevalence measures total existing cases. Hypertension is a chronic disease with many existing cases. It estimates the burden of disease in the community.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 17) Epidemiological methods are broadly divided into observational and:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Epidemiological methods include observational and experimental methods. Observational studies observe natural occurrence. Experimental studies involve intervention.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 18) Observational epidemiological studies include descriptive and:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Observational studies are descriptive or analytical. Descriptive studies describe disease occurrence. Analytical studies test association between exposure and outcome.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 19) Which is a descriptive epidemiological study?
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case report is a descriptive study. It describes an unusual or important single case. It does not test exposure-disease association formally.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 20) Case series means:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case series describes a group of similar cases. It is descriptive and does not include a formal comparison group. It may generate hypotheses for further study.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 21) Cross-sectional study observes the population at:
Epidemiology , Study design.option4: One point or short period of time
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at present time. It gives a snapshot of health status. It is useful for prevalence measurement.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 22) Cross-sectional study is most useful for measuring:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Cross-sectional study measures existing cases at a given time. Therefore, it is best for prevalence measurement. It cannot clearly establish temporal sequence.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 23) Ecological study uses:
Epidemiology , Study design.option3: Group or population as the unit
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Ecological study uses groups or populations as units of analysis. It compares population-level exposure and disease patterns. It may suggest associations but has risk of ecological fallacy.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 24) Analytical observational studies include case-control, cohort and:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Analytical observational studies test association between exposure and outcome. Case-control and cohort are major analytical designs. Analytical cross-sectional study can also assess association.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 25) Case-control study usually starts with:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case-control study starts with cases and controls. Past exposure is then compared between them. It is commonly retrospective.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 26) Case-control study is mostly:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case-control study usually looks backward from disease to exposure. It is efficient for rare diseases and long-latency diseases. It estimates odds ratio.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 27) Cohort study usually starts with:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Cohort study begins with exposure status. Exposed and unexposed groups are followed for outcome. It can measure incidence directly.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 28) Cohort study is commonly:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Cohort study follows people over time. It is commonly prospective, though retrospective cohort also exists. It is useful for incidence and natural history.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 29) Cohort study is useful for studying:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Cohort study can measure incidence because disease-free people are followed. It can study etiology and prognosis. It also helps observe natural history of disease.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 30) Case-control study is useful for studying:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case-control study compares exposure history among cases and controls. It assesses association between exposure and disease. It is commonly used when disease is rare.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 31) Clinical trial is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Clinical trial is an experimental study. It is longitudinal and always prospective. It is used to assess therapy and preventive measures.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 32) Clinical trial is mainly used to assess:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Clinical trial evaluates interventions. It may assess treatment, preventive drug or vaccine effect. Participants are followed prospectively.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 33) Randomized controlled trial belongs to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Randomized controlled trial is an experimental design. The investigator allocates intervention by randomization. It is strong for evaluating efficacy.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 34) Field trial usually involves:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Field trials are usually conducted among healthy individuals at risk. They often test preventive interventions. Vaccine trials are typical examples.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 35) Community trial usually has intervention applied to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Community trial applies intervention at community or group level. Examples include fluoridation or health education programmes. The unit may be a village, school or community.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 36) Quasi-experimental study differs from randomized trial mainly because it lacks:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Quasi-experimental study involves intervention but lacks randomization. It is useful when random allocation is impractical or unethical. It is weaker than randomized trial for causal inference.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 37) A study measuring current nutritional status of school children is most likely:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Current health status is assessed at one time. This fits cross-sectional design. It can estimate prevalence of undernutrition.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 38) A study following smokers and non-smokers for lung cancer is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: The study begins with exposure status: smokers and non-smokers. Then participants are followed for lung cancer. This is the classical cohort design.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 39) A study comparing past smoking history between lung cancer patients and controls is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: The study starts with disease status: cases and controls. Past exposure is then assessed. This is case-control study.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 40) Malaria constantly present in a defined area is called:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Endemic means constant presence of disease in a defined area. The frequency is relatively stable. Malaria in some regions is a common example.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 41) Sudden increase of dengue cases in Dhaka is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Epidemic means sudden increase above expected occurrence. It is usually localized to an area or population. Dengue outbreak in Dhaka is a typical example.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 42) COVID-19 spread across many countries is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Pandemic means worldwide or international spread. It affects large populations across countries. COVID-19 is a typical pandemic example.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 43) Interruption of transmission in a region while the agent exists elsewhere is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Elimination means interruption of transmission in a defined area. Control measures are still needed. The agent may exist elsewhere in the world.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 44) Termination of disease agent worldwide is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Eradication means disease agent is no longer present anywhere in the world. Routine control measures are no longer needed. Smallpox is the classical example.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 45) Smallpox is the classical example of:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Smallpox has been eradicated globally. This means the agent no longer circulates naturally anywhere. It is the standard example for eradication.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 46) Isolation is applied to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Isolation separates sick or infected individuals. The aim is to prevent spread from confirmed cases. It continues until the person becomes non-infectious.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 47) Quarantine is applied to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Quarantine restricts healthy but exposed people. They are not confirmed cases yet. It prevents spread if they develop disease later.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 48) Duration of quarantine is usually:
Epidemiology , Study design.option1: For the incubation period of disease
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Quarantine is maintained for the incubation period. This allows time to detect whether exposed persons develop disease. It is different from isolation of confirmed cases.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 49) Screening means presumptive identification of unrecognized disease among:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Screening detects hidden disease among apparently healthy people. It uses simple and rapid tests. Positive screening results require confirmation.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 50) Screening test is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Screening is presumptive identification. It does not give final diagnosis. Positive cases need confirmatory testing.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 51) A positive screening test should be followed by:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Screening only separates likely diseased from likely non-diseased. It is not diagnostic. Confirmatory testing establishes final diagnosis.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 52) Sensitivity of a test means ability to detect:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Sensitivity detects diseased persons correctly. High sensitivity means few false negatives. It is useful when missing disease is dangerous.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 53) Specificity of a test means ability to detect:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Specificity detects non-diseased persons correctly. High specificity means few false positives. It is useful to confirm or rule in disease.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 54) A highly sensitive test has:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: High sensitivity reduces false negatives. A negative result from a highly sensitive test helps rule out disease. This is useful in screening serious diseases.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 55) A highly specific test has:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: High specificity reduces false positives. A positive result from a highly specific test helps rule in disease. It is useful when false labeling is harmful.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 56) A sensitive test is especially useful to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: High sensitivity means few cases are missed. So a negative result is helpful for ruling out disease. This is remembered as SnNout.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 57) A specific test is especially useful to:
Epidemiology , Study design.option3: Rule out disease when negative only
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: High specificity means few false positives. Therefore, a positive result is more likely to be true. It helps rule in disease, remembered as SpPin. This is especially useful before labeling a person with a serious diagnosis.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 58) Positive predictive value means probability that a person with positive test actually:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Positive predictive value is the probability of disease among test-positive individuals. It depends on test performance and disease prevalence. When prevalence rises, positive predictive value usually rises. It answers the patient-centered question: “If positive, what is the chance I truly have disease?”

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 59) Negative predictive value means probability that a person with negative test actually:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Negative predictive value is the probability of being disease-free among test-negative individuals. It increases when disease prevalence is low. It depends on sensitivity, specificity and prevalence. It answers: “If negative, what is the chance I truly do not have disease?”

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 60) When disease prevalence increases, positive predictive value generally:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Positive predictive value rises with disease prevalence. When disease is common, a positive test is more likely to represent true disease. When disease is rare, false positives form a larger share of positive results. This is why screening performance depends on population selection.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 61) Attack rate is best described as:
Epidemiology , Study design.option2: Ratio of male to female cases
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Attack rate is a form of incidence used in outbreaks. It measures proportion of exposed or at-risk people who develop disease. It is often used in food poisoning and epidemic investigations. It helps identify the likely exposure responsible for an outbreak.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 62) Relative risk is usually calculated in:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Relative risk compares incidence among exposed and unexposed groups. Cohort study can measure incidence directly. Therefore, relative risk is commonly calculated from cohort studies. A relative risk above 1 suggests positive association with exposure.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 63) Odds ratio is classically calculated in:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case-control study begins with disease status, so incidence cannot be directly calculated. Odds ratio compares odds of exposure among cases and controls. It is the standard association measure in case-control studies. For rare diseases, odds ratio approximates relative risk.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 64) Randomization in a clinical trial mainly helps to:
Epidemiology , Study design.option3: Reduce selection bias and balance confounders
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Randomization gives each participant a known chance of receiving either intervention. It helps make comparison groups similar at baseline. This reduces selection bias and balances known and unknown confounders. It increases validity of treatment comparison.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 65) Blinding in a trial is mainly used to reduce:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Blinding prevents participants, investigators or assessors from knowing allocation. It reduces biased reporting, treatment behaviour and outcome assessment. Single, double and triple blinding may be used. Blinding improves objectivity in clinical trials.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 66) Confounding occurs when:
Epidemiology , Study design.option2: A third factor distorts exposure-disease association
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Confounding occurs when another variable is linked to both exposure and outcome. It can create, hide or exaggerate an association. For example, age may confound relation between exercise and heart disease. Control methods include restriction, matching, stratification and multivariable analysis.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 67) Bias in epidemiology means:
Epidemiology , Study design.option1: Systematic error in design, conduct or analysis
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Bias is a systematic error that produces an incorrect estimate. It can occur during selection, information collection or analysis. Unlike random error, increasing sample size does not automatically remove bias. Good study design is essential to minimize it.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 68) Lead time bias is most relevant to:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Lead time bias occurs when early detection appears to prolong survival without actually delaying death. It can make screening look more beneficial than it truly is. Survival time increases from earlier diagnosis, not necessarily from longer life. Mortality reduction is a better outcome for screening effectiveness.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 69) The best epidemiological study for rare disease with long latent period is usually:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Case-control study is efficient for rare diseases. It starts with diseased cases and compares their past exposure with controls. It is also useful for diseases with long latency, such as many cancers. It saves time and resources compared with following a large cohort.

Epidemiology , Study design.question: 70) The strongest design for testing efficacy of a new drug is:
Epidemiology , Study design.exp: Randomized controlled trial is strongest for testing treatment efficacy. Random allocation reduces selection bias and balances confounders. Blinding and control groups further improve validity. It provides high-quality evidence when ethical and feasible.
